```{r load-data}
clean        <- readRDS(here::here("data/clean/cu_sl_st_clean.rds"))
pca_results  <- readRDS(here::here("data/clean/pca_results.rds"))
gmm_results  <- readRDS(here::here("data/clean/gmm_results.rds"))
jags_results <- readRDS(here::here("data/clean/jags_results.rds"))

n_pitches  <- nrow(clean)
n_pitchers <- n_distinct(clean$pitcher)
n_cu <- sum(clean$pitch_type == "CU")
n_sl <- sum(clean$pitch_type == "SL")
n_st <- sum(clean$pitch_type == "ST")
years <- "2022–2024"
```

# Introduction

Major League Baseball's Statcast system classifies every pitch into a discrete
category. For breaking balls, three labels are currently in use: the curveball
(`CU`), the slider (`SL`), and the sweeper (`ST`). Each occupies a distinct
niche in broadcast and analytics discourse — curveballs are described as
high-drop "12-to-6" pitches, sliders as sharper and more horizontal, and
sweepers as the extreme horizontal-break variant that has reshaped modern
pitching strategy.

But these descriptions trace a continuum, not three separate populations.  The
movement space from curveball to sweeper — decreasing vertical drop, increasing
horizontal break — is theoretically smooth, and there is no obvious physical
reason why a pitch at any intermediate point should belong unambiguously to one
label or another.  The sweeper label itself is recent: Statcast introduced `ST`
around 2022–2023, reclassifying pitches that had previously been called sliders.
Before that boundary was drawn, no one argued those pitches were categorically
different from the sliders around them.

This study asks whether the three-label breaking-ball taxonomy is empirically
justified.  We apply three complementary analyses to
`r format(n_pitches, big.mark = ",")` CU, SL, and ST pitches thrown by
`r n_pitchers` pitchers from `r years`:

1. **PCA** to visualize the structure of movement space;
2. **GMM** to formally test whether the data support three natural clusters;
3. **Bayesian hierarchical regression** to test whether the labels predict
   outcomes — whiff rate, chase rate, and wOBA against — above and beyond the
   movement features themselves.

# Historical Context

This is not the first time a Statcast classification boundary has been
contested. The sinker (`SI`) and two-seam fastball (`FT`) coexisted as distinct
labels from the introduction of Statcast through approximately 2020, despite
substantial overlap in their movement profiles [@dvorocsik2019]. MLB eventually
deprecated `FT`, absorbing two-seamers into the sinker category. The
sabermetric community had anticipated this — empirically, the two types were
never geometrically separable.

The sweeper presents the same question, but in the opposite direction: a label
was *added* rather than removed, drawing a new boundary inside what had
previously been a single category. Whether that boundary reflects a real
discontinuity in pitch characteristics and outcomes — or whether it is a
taxonomic artifact of an evolving algorithmic classifier — is the question this
paper addresses.

# Research Question

**Does the CU/SL/ST pitch label predict outcomes above and beyond the movement
features themselves?**

We decompose this into two sub-questions:

1. **Geometric:** Does the movement–speed space of breaking balls contain three
   natural clusters that align with the CU/SL/ST labels, or does it form a
   single elongated continuum?
2. **Predictive:** After conditioning on movement features (horizontal break,
   induced vertical break, velocity), does knowing the pitch label tell us
   anything additional about whiff rate, chase rate, or wOBA against?

If the answer to both is no, the breaking-ball taxonomy is unsupported.

# Data

Data come from MLB Statcast via Baseball Savant, accessed through the
`baseballr` R package [@baumer2023].  We retain all pitches classified as CU,
SL, or ST from regular-season games in `r years`
(CU: `r format(n_cu, big.mark = ",")`; SL: `r format(n_sl, big.mark = ",")`;
ST: `r format(n_st, big.mark = ",")`). The sample begins in 2022 because the
`ST` label did not exist before then.

**Key variables:**

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| `pitch_type` | CU, SL, or ST |
| `pfx_x` | Horizontal movement (inches, relative to gyroball) |
| `pfx_z` | Induced vertical break (inches) |
| `release_speed` | Velocity at release (mph) |
| `release_spin_rate` | Spin rate (rpm) |
| `release_spin_axis` | Spin axis (degrees) |
| `p_throws` | Pitcher handedness (L/R) |

**Preprocessing:** `pfx_x` is sign-flipped for left-handed pitchers so that
glove-side break is consistently directed regardless of handedness.  After
adjustment, arm-side movement is positive and glove-side movement (the dominant
direction for all three pitch types) is negative.  All three movement/speed
features are standardized ($\mu = 0$, $\sigma = 1$) before modelling.
Spin axis is standardized and available as an optional fourth feature.

**Outcomes:**

- **Whiff** (binary): swing-and-miss or foul-tip.
- **Chase** (binary): swing at an out-of-zone pitch (zones 11–14); NA for
  in-zone pitches.
- **wOBA against** (continuous): linear-weight wOBA for PA-ending pitches,
  using `r years` average weights.

# Stage 1: Principal Component Analysis

## Method

We apply PCA to the three standardized features (pfx\_x, pfx\_z, release
speed) to characterize the shape of breaking-ball movement space.  The
continuum hypothesis predicts that PC1 will capture the trade-off between
vertical drop (curveball end) and horizontal break (sweeper end), producing one
elongated cloud rather than three distinct clusters.

## Results

```{r pca-summary}
var1 <- round(pca_results$var_exp[1] * 100, 1)
var2 <- round(pca_results$var_exp[2] * 100, 1)
cum2 <- round(pca_results$cum_var[2] * 100, 1)
```

PC1 explains `r var1`% of variance; PC1 and PC2 together explain `r cum2`%.
The PCA biplot (Figure \@ref(fig:fig-f2)) shows
`r if(cum2 > 85) "a single elongated cloud" else "the primary structure"` in
breaking-ball movement space.

```{r pca-loadings}
ldg <- as.data.frame(round(pca_results$pca$rotation[, 1:3], 3)) |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("Feature") |>
  mutate(Feature = recode(Feature,
    pfx_x_z = "Horiz. break (pfx\\_x, adj.)",
    pfx_z_z = "Vert. break (pfx\\_z)",
    speed_z = "Release speed"))
```

```{r pca-tab}
kable(
  ldg,
  caption = "PCA loadings for the first three principal components.",
  booktabs = TRUE
) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position")
```

```{r fig-f1, fig.cap="Movement profiles for CU (blue), SL (orange), and ST (green). pfx\\_x is sign-flipped for LHP so glove-side break is consistently negative."}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/F1_movement_scatter.png")
```

```{r fig-f2, fig.cap="PCA biplot of breaking-ball movement space. Arrows show feature loadings scaled to the score cloud. A single elongated cloud would support the continuum hypothesis; three well-separated regions would support distinct categories."}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/F2_pca_biplot.png")
```

# Stage 2: Gaussian Mixture Modelling

## Method

We fit GMMs via `mclust` [@scrucca2016] to the three standardized features,
selecting the number of components $G \in \{2,\ldots,8\}$ and covariance
parameterization jointly by BIC.  Three solutions are reported:

- **Forced G = 2**: is there a single split?
- **Forced G = 3**: do three clusters recover the CU/SL/ST labels?
- **BIC-optimal**: what does the data prefer?

Cluster–label alignment is quantified by the ARI [@hubert1985].

## Results

```{r gmm-summary}
g_opt    <- gmm_results$fit_bic$G
mod_name <- gmm_results$fit_bic$modelName
ari_g2   <- round(gmm_results$ari_g2, 3)
ari_g3   <- round(gmm_results$ari_g3, 3)
ari_bic  <- round(gmm_results$ari_bic, 3)
pur_g3   <- round(gmm_results$purity_g3, 3)
```

The BIC-optimal solution selected $G = `r g_opt`$ components
(model `r mod_name`).  The forced $G = 3$ solution yields ARI = `r ari_g3`
against the three Statcast labels (Table \@ref(tab:gmm-tab-g3)); the forced
$G = 2$ solution yields ARI = `r ari_g2`; the BIC-optimal yields ARI =
`r ari_bic`.  Cluster purity for the forced $G = 3$ solution is `r pur_g3`.

```{r gmm-tab-g3}
tab_df <- as.data.frame.matrix(gmm_results$tab_g3)
kable(
  tab_df,
  caption = "Contingency table: GMM clusters (forced G=3) vs. Statcast label.",
  booktabs = TRUE
) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position")
```

```{r fig-f3, fig.cap="GMM clusters (forced G=3) coloured by Statcast label. If the three clusters align with CU/SL/ST, each panel should be dominated by one colour."}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/F3_gmm_g3_vs_label.png")
```

```{r fig-f4, fig.cap="BIC as a function of GMM components. The dashed red line marks the BIC-optimal solution."}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/F4_bic_curve.png")
```

# Stage 3: Bayesian Hierarchical Model

## Model

For each outcome $y_i$ (pitch $i$ thrown by pitcher $j[i]$):

$$g(\mathbb{E}[y_i]) = \alpha_{j[i]} + \beta_x \tilde{x}_i + \beta_z \tilde{z}_i + \beta_v \tilde{v}_i + \beta_{\text{SL}} \cdot \mathbf{1}[\text{SL}]_i + \beta_{\text{ST}} \cdot \mathbf{1}[\text{ST}]_i$$

$$\alpha_j \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_\alpha,\; \tau_\alpha^{-1})$$

CU is the reference category; $\mathbf{1}[\text{SL}]$ and
$\mathbf{1}[\text{ST}]$ are binary indicators.  $g$ is the logit link for
whiff and chase, and the identity link for wOBA.  A pitcher random intercept
$\alpha_j$ accounts for between-pitcher differences in breaking-ball usage.

The three key estimands are:
- $\beta_{\text{SL}}$: slider vs. curveball effect, controlling for movement;
- $\beta_{\text{ST}}$: sweeper vs. curveball effect, controlling for movement;
- $\beta_{\text{ST}} - \beta_{\text{SL}}$: sweeper vs. slider contrast,
  computed as a derived quantity inside JAGS.

## Priors

Following @kery2012:

$$\beta_k \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\; 0.001^{-1}), \quad \mu_\alpha \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\; 0.001^{-1}), \quad \tau_\alpha,\, \tau \sim \text{Gamma}(0.001,\; 0.001)$$

## Inference

Three chains, 5,000 burn-in, thinned by 5, via `jagsUI` [@kellner2021].
Convergence: $\hat{R} < 1.1$ for all nodes.

## Results

```{r label-tab-data}
get_label_rows <- function(fit, outcome) {
  betas  <- c("beta_sl", "beta_st", "beta_st_vs_sl")
  labels <- c("SL vs. CU", "ST vs. CU", "ST vs. SL")
  rows <- lapply(seq_along(betas), function(i) {
    b    <- betas[i]
    s    <- fit$summary[b, ]
    rhat <- fit$Rhat[[b]]
    data.frame(
      Outcome  = outcome,
      Contrast = labels[i],
      Mean     = round(s["mean"], 3),
      SD       = round(s["sd"],   3),
      `2.5%`   = round(s["2.5%"], 3),
      `97.5%`  = round(s["97.5%"], 3),
      Rhat     = round(rhat, 3),
      check.names = FALSE
    )
  })
  do.call(rbind, rows)
}

label_tab <- bind_rows(
  get_label_rows(jags_results$fit_whiff, "Whiff rate"),
  get_label_rows(jags_results$fit_chase, "Chase rate"),
  get_label_rows(jags_results$fit_woba,  "wOBA against")
)
```

```{r label-tab-print}
kable(
  label_tab |> select(-Outcome),
  col.names = c("Contrast", "Mean", "SD", "2.5%", "97.5%", "$\\hat{R}$"),
  caption   = paste(
    "Posterior summaries for label contrasts across three outcome models.",
    "Reference category is CU. $\\hat{R} < 1.1$ throughout indicates convergence.",
    "Credible intervals that include zero indicate no evidence for predictive",
    "value of the label beyond movement."
  ),
  booktabs = TRUE,
  escape   = FALSE
) |>
  pack_rows("Whiff rate", 1, 3) |>
  pack_rows("Chase rate", 4, 6) |>
  pack_rows("wOBA against", 7, 9) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position", "scale_down"))
```

```{r fig-f5, fig.cap="Posterior densities for the three pairwise label contrasts (columns) across three outcomes (rows). The dashed line marks zero. Distributions centred on zero with intervals straddling zero indicate the labels add no predictive information beyond movement."}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/F5_beta_posteriors.png")
```

```{r fig-f6, fig.cap="Top and bottom 20 pitcher random intercepts from the whiff model (95\\% credible intervals). Large between-pitcher variation motivates the partial-pooling structure."}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/F6_pitcher_intercepts.png")
```

# Discussion

The three-stage analysis provides a coherent answer to whether the CU/SL/ST
taxonomy is empirically justified.  If the PCA cloud is elongated rather than
trimodal, the GMM prefers $G \neq 3$ or yields low ARI at $G = 3$, and the
posterior distributions of $\beta_{\text{SL}}$, $\beta_{\text{ST}}$, and
$\beta_{\text{ST}} - \beta_{\text{SL}}$ are all centred near zero — the
taxonomy is a continuum, not three distinct categories.

A finding that the labels *do* carry predictive information after controlling
for movement would be equally interpretable: it would mean that pitchers
classified as sweeper-throwers deploy their pitches in systematically different
counts, locations, or matchups in ways that produce different outcomes
regardless of the movement profile — suggesting that the label captures
something real about pitcher strategy, even if the movement profiles overlap.

**Limitations.** (1) The `ST` label was introduced mid-way through 2022,
creating potential measurement error in the first data-year: pitches that
would now be labeled ST may still carry the SL label from early 2022.
Restricting to 2023–2024 is a natural sensitivity check. (2) The wOBA
model pools across all count situations; count-stratified analyses may reveal
heterogeneity masked here. (3) Chase rate conditions on out-of-zone pitches,
which are not randomly assigned — pitchers and batters select into this sample
— introducing potential collider bias. (4) The Kéry & Schaub flat priors on
precisions are standard in ecological applications; their behavior on the
logit scale for this sample size warrants sensitivity analysis.

# Conclusion

Whether the curveball, slider, and sweeper represent meaningfully distinct pitch
types — or whether they are three names for points on a continuum of horizontal
versus vertical break — is an empirical question with real consequences for
player evaluation, pitch design, and sports analytics research. This study
provides a principled three-stage framework for answering it. The results bear
directly on whether analysts and front offices should treat these pitch types
as categorically distinct inputs in outcome models, or whether continuous
movement features are the more appropriate representation.
